text:
Recent work supports testing which historical interactions change recommendations. [Demystifying Sequential Recommendations (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) searches for minimal history edits that alter recommendations using genetic algorithms; useful precedent for deletion/replacement probes, though optimized edits differ from controlled diagnostics. [CoDeR (AAAI 2025)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/33379) models short-sequence demand shifts and distinguishes them from noise under its causal assumptions. [CoDeR+ (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3778863) extends this approach with interest-aware counterfactual reasoning. These works motivate separating recent intent from persistent preferences; their causal terminology does not make arbitrary history perturbations causal evidence.

A practical diagnostic design follows from these ideas: reserve training suffixes as prediction targets, then compare paired original/perturbed prefixes using fixed candidates. Shuffle items while preserving multiplicities to test order sensitivity; delete equally sized recent versus older windows to test recency; remove repeated-interest interactions versus frequency-matched controls to test reliance on repetition. Report paired target-rank changes, HR@10 changes, and recommendation overlap, stratified by history length and target popularity. Compare attribution-guided deletion against random and recency-based deletion, and test whether retaining attributed interactions preserves predictions. A [2026 temporal-attribution study](https://jidmis.org/index.php/jidmis/article/view/2525) evaluates related faithfulness, sufficiency, and mask-versus-shuffle checks. Interpretation remains diagnostic: weak shuffle sensitivity can motivate position-encoding checks; excessive last-item dependence can motivate aggregation or recency-weight changes. Control padding, sequence length, position reassignment, and item frequency before attributing effects to temporal reasoning; sensitivity demonstrates model dependence, not causal changes in user preferences.
